title: Absolute Zero: The Coldest Possible Temperature
hook: There's no limit to how hot things can get, but cold has a floor. At absolute zero, −273°C, particle motion bottoms out — and you can get achingly close but never quite reach it.
key_points: Temperature tracks particle motion; absolute zero is where that motion is minimal.
It sits at 0 kelvin, about −273.15°C — the bottom of the temperature scale.
You can approach it ever more closely but never fully reach it (third law of thermodynamics).
Near absolute zero, matter does strange things like superconducting and forming new states.
content_html: Temperature is really a measure of how much the particles in a substance are jiggling — the faster they move, the hotter it is. That immediately suggests a floor: there must be a point where that motion is as low as it can go. That point is absolute zero, which sits at 0 on the kelvin scale, about −273.15°C. It's why scientists prefer kelvin: it starts at the true bottom, so a temperature in kelvin is directly proportional to particle energy.
extra_html: Curiously, while there's no upper limit on temperature — you can always pump in more energy — absolute zero can never actually be reached. The third law of thermodynamics says you can only approach it in ever-smaller steps, never arriving; the closest labs have come is within a few billionths of a degree. (Even there, quantum physics insists particles keep a tiny irreducible jitter.) The deep cold is worth chasing because matter turns strange near it: some metals lose all electrical resistance and become superconductors, helium flows without friction as a superfluid, and atoms can merge into a single quantum blob called a Bose–Einstein condensate. Wikipedia covers the scale, the third law, and these exotic states.

related.title: Heat vs. Temperature
related.hook: A sparkler can hit thousands of degrees yet barely burn you — because temperature and heat are not the same thing.

related.title: States of Matter
related.hook: Solid, liquid, gas, plasma — the difference is how tightly particles are bound. Add heat and matter changes state, but during the change the temperature holds still.

related.title: Entropy & the Arrow of Time
related.hook: Why does a smashed cup never reassemble itself? The second law of thermodynamics says disorder almost always wins.

flashcards.back_html: The lowest possible temperature — 0 kelvin (about −273°C) — where the motion of particles drops to its absolute minimum.

flashcards.prompt: Why is there a coldest possible temperature but no hottest?

choices.text: Temperature reflects particle motion, which can't go below a minimum but can always increase
Cold is a substance that eventually runs out

flashcards.explanation_html: You can always add more energy and motion, but you can't remove more than all of it. Absolute zero is where motion bottoms out.

flashcards.prompt: Can scientists actually cool something all the way to absolute zero?

choices.text: No — they can get extraordinarily close but never quite reach it
Yes, it's done routinely in freezers
Yes, but only in outer space

flashcards.explanation_html: The third law of thermodynamics implies absolute zero is unreachable in a finite number of steps; labs have come to within billionths of a degree.
